opus_only: Watching many markets instead of one gives more opportunities, because when one market is quiet another may be moving; this drove his move to a multi-market commodity broker.
He aimed to make money from outside the markets (trading as an outsider with a method) rather than as an establishment insider; he notes others who tried often failed.
Direct, hands-on empirical contact with data (rather than viewing a screen that looks like random noise) shaped his belief in trends.
The early Brockham system suffered severe losses in cotton, causing the family split (single-market loss risk in a rule-based system).
Their testing software was far ahead of City institutions' tools, a technology edge used in marketing.
Efficient-market (Brownian motion) theory became the basis of bank risk management and the derivatives boom, which he says ended up destroying the economy.
Using derivative-pricing math to price instruments and sell at a markup is merchandising with no interest in whether the model fits reality; he contrasts it with studying the underlying reality.
Banks then sold overpriced derivatives for fifteen years to clients such as Orange County and Italian municipalities; he calls his 1993 talk prescient.
Most quants used efficient market theory to price derivatives; trend following was a narrow sideline.
Persistent positive returns eventually attract capital, but slowly because returns are not smooth.
The financial establishment (bankers, managers, professors, consultants, CFAs) holds theory A (efficiency); trend followers hold theory B, testable because you can bet on the difference.
CTA money came from commodity brokers (Shearson, E.F. Hutton, Merrill, Man); from the late 1990s the hedge fund world mostly did not accept CTAs as hedge funds.
Big macro funds (Moore/Bacon, Tudor Jones, Caxton/Kovner) also came from commodity backgrounds.
Investors swing between extremes: commodities went from 'terminally dull' to 'terribly exciting'.
Goldman took a 10% stake in Winton a week before the August 2007 quant quake, in which Goldman's Global Alpha blew up.
Credit cracked first (August 2007); US stocks peaked only in October-November 2007 and emerging markets went higher still, so equity weakness lagged credit.
After 2008 the investor base became conspicuously institutional (pension funds, endowments).
Even at 1 and 20, the product is more expensive than optimal for clients once distribution fees are added.
There are about 1,000 liquid equity markets (e.g. Apple, GE, Exxon) to diversify into, though not all are deep.
Trend following is mathematics applied to professional gambling on prices; statistics sets the odds, like Buffett's 'handicapping'.
The research operation is about programming and computer testing; the leader need not program himself.
Academic finance journals (JF, J Portfolio Management, J Forecasting, J Futures Markets) cover what Winton researchers do, but are disconnected, not one coherent project.
Interviewer reports that Winton studied whether the market did worse when it rained in London; Harding says that is purely statistical research.
Maths is useful for making better inferences, but finance is not physics.
A cap-weighted index like the S&P 500 is itself a trading system: long 500 stocks, adding and removing them by rules.
Beating long-only indexes by even 1-20 bp would be worth billions, and is a highly soluble maths problem.
The index works because minimizing transaction costs and owning everything beats most active managers.
A long-only index-enhancement business earns management fees, valued at a much higher P/E than performance fees, and diversifies income.
Investments always get oversold, so a small real edge tends to be marketed as larger.
The investment process must keep changing because finance is not a physical problem.
The S&P 500 has not worked for the last fifteen years (about 1998-2013).
The index has been widely gamed: traders buy stocks before inclusion and sell before deletion, adding to public investors' losses.
sonnet_only: Moving from a single market (gilts) to many markets gave more chances for patterns and was the start of his multi-market approach.
Harding reasons that something may be happening in another market when one is quiet, so a larger market set offers more opportunity.
Harding asserts his data could have definitively disproved efficient-market theory.
Harding criticizes banks' use of financial mathematics to price derivatives from a model and sell at a markup, since it does not test whether the model matches market reality.
Winton (set up 1997) started as a trend-following CTA because Harding already knew how to run those systems.
Trend-following theory (B) versus the mainstream efficient-market theory (A) differ testably through performance of trading each way.
Investing is handicapping: work out the odds and bet accordingly (Buffett's term).
Harding thinks mathematical methods could beat a cap-weighted index like the S&P 500 by about 20 basis points, which would be worth billions in fees.
Harding says the S&P 500 index approach has been exploited by traders who buy before index additions and sell before deletions, hurting index investors.
